questions.prompt: Compare PPO-based RLHF with DPO for aligning a chat model: what does each optimize, and when would you pick one over the other?
questions.modelAnswer: RLHF is a two-stage pipeline: fit a reward model on human preference pairs, then run PPO to maximize that reward with a KL penalty keeping the policy near the reference model. It is flexible and online - the policy samples fresh outputs and can be pushed beyond the preference data's support - but operationally heavy: policy, reference, reward model, and value function in memory, PPO's hyperparameter fragility, and reward hacking as a standing threat. DPO collapses the pipeline: for the same KL-regularized objective there is a closed-form relationship between the optimal policy and the reward, so you can optimize the policy directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss - no reward model, no sampling loop, dramatically simpler and more stable. Its limits are the mirror image: it is offline, bound to the support and quality of the preference dataset, and can drift if the data is far off-policy. Practical rule: DPO and its variants for most teams and most fine-tunes; online RL when you have the infrastructure and need to optimize against a reward signal beyond static pairs. In both cases the binding constraint is preference-data quality and evaluation coverage, not the algorithm.
rubric: Describes both objectives correctly, including the KL anchor to the reference model
States DPO's key move: closed-form policy-reward relation removing the reward model
Gives the online-vs-offline trade-off honestly in both directions
Lands on a defensible selection rule and names data quality as the binding constraint
followUps: What does reward hacking look like in practice, and which guardrails catch it?

questions.prompt: You serve a 70B model and want to cut serving cost with quantization. Design the approach: what do you quantize, with which class of method, and how do you validate it?
questions.modelAnswer: First separate the two regimes. Weight-only quantization (int4 GPTQ/AWQ-class) shrinks memory about 4x versus fp16 and speeds up decode, which is memory-bandwidth-bound - ideal when you are capacity- or VRAM-constrained. Weight-and-activation quantization (fp8 on Hopper-class hardware, or SmoothQuant-style int8) engages faster tensor-core math, accelerating compute-bound prefill too - the better default when you control modern hardware. My plan: fp8 W8A8 as the baseline on H100s, int4 weight-only where memory is the binding constraint; keep the sensitive pieces - embeddings, lm_head, and often the first and last blocks - at higher precision, and quantize the KV cache to fp8 as a separate, composable lever. Validation is where quantization efforts fail: perplexity deltas are necessary but not sufficient, so run the full task-eval suite plus format and safety regressions against the fp16 baseline and inspect per-task deltas, because long-tail degradation - non-English, math, strict-format outputs - hides inside healthy aggregates. Then benchmark end-to-end throughput and latency to confirm the win is real on your serving stack, and roll out behind a flag with quality monitors and an A/B, keeping instant rollback to the fp16 path.
rubric: Distinguishes weight-only vs weight+activation and maps each to decode vs prefill economics
Keeps sensitive components at higher precision and treats KV quantization as separate
Validation goes beyond perplexity to per-task, format, and safety regressions
Confirms the cost win with end-to-end benchmarks and ships behind a flag with rollback
followUps: Why do outlier activation channels make int8 activation quantization hard?

questions.prompt: Design an LLM inference service to hold TTFT p95 under 500ms and inter-token p95 under 50ms at 100 requests per second. Cover batching, scheduling, and capacity planning.
questions.modelAnswer: Anchor on the two-phase reality: prefill is compute-bound and produces TTFT; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and produces inter-token latency - one SLO per phase, so measure and protect them separately. The core throughput mechanism is continuous batching: the scheduler admits and retires requests at token-step granularity, so new arrivals join between decode iterations instead of waiting for a static batch to drain. The tension is that a long prefill inserted into the decode loop stalls every in-flight request's next token, so chunk prefills into slices interleaved with decode steps, and at scale disaggregate - separate prefill and decode pools with KV handoff - to isolate the SLOs completely. Memory: paged KV cache to prevent fragmentation, and admission control against a KV budget so overload queues at the door rather than OOMing mid-stream. Capacity: benchmark one replica for tokens/sec and max concurrent sequences at the target latency point - not at max throughput, which sits past the latency knee - then provision for peak with headroom and autoscale on queue depth and KV utilization, draining connections on scale-down. Add prompt caching for shared prefixes, priority classes with a dedicated long-context pool so heavy requests cannot blow the p95, and load-shedding that rejects early with a clear signal. Observability: per-phase histograms of TTFT and TPOT, KV occupancy, preemption counts, and queue depth - these are the dials the on-call actually turns.
rubric: Separates prefill/TTFT from decode/TPOT and treats them as distinct SLOs
Explains continuous batching and the prefill-stalls-decode tension with a mitigation
Uses paged KV plus KV-budget admission control to fail at the door, not mid-stream
Capacity is benchmarked at the latency point with autoscaling on leading signals
Includes priority isolation for long-context and per-phase observability
followUps: Where does speculative decoding fit, and what does it do to your capacity math?

questions.prompt: Your benchmark shows TTFT holding steady but inter-token latency degrading 3x once concurrency passes 16. What is happening, and how do you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: The signature points at the decode path: every decode step processes the whole batch, and each step must read every sequence's KV cache, so total KV bytes read per token-step grows with concurrency - past a knee you saturate memory bandwidth and per-token time climbs while prefill (compute-bound, unchanged) keeps TTFT flat. Three specific suspects: pure bandwidth saturation from aggregate KV size; KV-cache pressure triggering preemptions or swapping, which shows up as latency spikes rather than smooth degradation - check the engine's preemption and eviction counters; and prefill interleaving stalling decode if chunked prefill is off, though that usually moves TTFT too. Confirm by measurement: sweep concurrency and plot per-token latency against total batched tokens - a bandwidth story bends at a predictable knee; profile with DCGM or Nsight expecting high memory-bandwidth utilization with comparatively low SM occupancy during decode; and correlate the latency curve with KV occupancy and preemption metrics. Fixes follow the diagnosis: cap max batched tokens per step to bound worst-case step time, enable chunked prefill, shrink KV traffic with GQA or fp8 KV quantization, or accept the knee as your per-replica capacity and scale out - often the honest answer is that 16 concurrent sequences is simply this hardware's operating point.
rubric: Explains why decode degrades with batch KV growth while TTFT stays flat
Separates smooth bandwidth saturation from spiky preemption/eviction behavior
Confirms with profiler evidence: bandwidth-bound decode, preemption counters, latency-vs-tokens curve
Fixes match the mechanism, including accepting the knee as capacity
followUps: How would you design the benchmark to find this knee before production did?

questions.prompt: An hour after a routine deploy, your self-hosted LLM API starts throwing intermittent CUDA OOMs and occasionally garbled outputs. Walk through your incident response.
questions.modelAnswer: Mitigate first: roll back the deploy - a failure starting an hour after a change is presumed caused by it until proven otherwise - and recycle the affected replicas rather than trusting them, because a process that has hit CUDA OOM can be left with a corrupted allocator or fragmented memory, and garbled output from a wounded process does not heal on its own. If rollback is blocked, reduce pressure: cut max concurrency and max context so requests stop landing past the memory budget. Then diagnose from the diff and the telemetry: what changed - engine version, weights, or config - with special suspicion of lost admission-control settings (max batched tokens, KV budget), since 'intermittent OOM correlated with request mix' is exactly what missing admission control looks like; the hour of delay fits memory pressure building to the tipping point. Garbled output alongside memory errors widens the net: dtype or quantization mismatch on new weights, kernel/driver incompatibility, or hardware ECC errors - check dmesg and DCGM to rule the hardware in or out. Verify recovery with a canary replaying captured traffic plus golden-prompt output checks, not just error rates, since silent corruption is the scarier half of this incident. Postmortem: deploy gates get a memory-pressure load test and output-equivalence checks, and admission-control config becomes validated, versioned, and impossible to lose in a deploy.
rubric: Rolls back and recycles replicas, with the corrupted-process rationale
Connects intermittent OOM to lost admission control and the delayed onset to pressure buildup
Treats garbled output as its own signal: dtype/quantization mismatch or hardware, checked via dmesg/DCGM
Verifies with golden-output checks, not error rates alone, and hardens the deploy gate
followUps: What belongs in a pre-deploy load test to catch this class of regression?

questions.prompt: Given a large stream of events, return the k most frequent event types. Talk through your approach and its complexity - then how it changes when the counts no longer fit in memory.
questions.modelAnswer: In-memory: one pass building a hash map of counts, O(n) time, O(u) space for u unique types; then select the top k with a min-heap of size k - iterate the counts, push, and pop the minimum whenever the heap exceeds k - for O(u log k) selection and O(k) extra space, which beats a full O(u log u) sort when k is much smaller than u. A bucket-by-count array gives O(n + u) exact selection if you want to avoid the log factor. When counts exceed memory: partition by hash of the key across files or machines so every occurrence of a key lands in one shard, count exactly per shard, take each shard's top k, and merge - correct because a global top-k element must be a top-k element of its own shard. If it is a true unbounded stream, trade exactness for space: a Count-Min Sketch plus a k-sized heap gives bounded memory with one-sided overcount error, acceptable for trend detection but not for billing. I would also clarify requirements up front: tie handling, batch versus streaming, and whether approximate answers are acceptable - that last one halves the design space.
rubric: Correct O(n) counting plus O(u log k) heap selection with the k << u justification
Sharding argument is stated: hash partitioning makes per-shard top-k merge correct
Knows the exact/approximate boundary and what Count-Min error semantics allow
Surfaces clarifying assumptions: ties, streaming, exactness requirements
followUps: Why does taking each shard's top k stay correct, and when would it break?

questions.prompt: Design the public REST API for a model-inference platform: endpoints, versioning, sync versus async, and failure semantics.
questions.modelAnswer: Core resource: POST /v1/models/{model}/predictions. API version lives in the path and only breaking changes bump it; within a version, changes are additive. Model versions are a separate axis: callers may pin one explicitly, and every response echoes the resolved version so results are attributable and reproducible. Sync versus async by latency class: fast models answer synchronously under a hard timeout; long-running work returns 202 with a job resource - GET /v1/jobs/{id} for polling, webhooks for push - because holding connections for minutes fails at every proxy and mobile network between you and the caller. Failure semantics get designed, not inherited: idempotency keys on POST so client retries cannot double-execute or double-bill; a correct 4xx/5xx split - 400 validation, 401/403 auth, 429 rate-limited with Retry-After, 503 overloaded - because clients build retry logic off these codes; structured error bodies with stable machine-readable codes and a request ID for support. Round it out with pagination on list endpoints, per-key quotas and rate limits, published SLOs, and contract tests in CI so a 'small' response change cannot break integrators silently.
rubric: Separates API versioning from model versioning, echoing the resolved model version
Async pattern is correct: 202 plus job resource, with the connection-holding rationale
Idempotency keys and a deliberate 4xx/5xx mapping with Retry-After on 429
Includes observability and compatibility: request IDs, contract tests, SLOs
followUps: How would you introduce streaming responses without breaking existing clients?

questions.prompt: From a client typing an API URL to receiving JSON - walk through what happens at the network level, and how the layers map to the failures you see in production.
questions.modelAnswer: DNS first: local and OS caches, then a recursive resolver walks to the authoritative server, returning an IP. TCP handshake next - SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK - establishing a reliable byte stream. For HTTPS, the TLS handshake follows: negotiate protocol version and cipher, the server presents a certificate the client validates against trusted CAs and the hostname, and the two derive session keys. Only then does the HTTP request travel over the encrypted stream, typically hitting a load balancer that forwards to an application server, which returns status, headers, and JSON body. Connection reuse via keep-alive, and multiplexing in HTTP/2, exist to amortize those handshakes - and the request usually rides an already-open connection. The production value of this model is that failures name their layer: NXDOMAIN or resolution timeouts are DNS; connection refused or timeout is TCP - a dead service, a closed port, a firewall, or a security-group rule; certificate errors are TLS - expiry, hostname mismatch, or a missing chain; 4xx/5xx means the network is fine and the application is not. Debugging an outage is walking that ladder in order.
rubric: Covers DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP in order with the essential purpose of each
Includes cert validation and where keep-alive/multiplexing fit
Maps failure symptoms to layers as a debugging ladder
Stays concise and correctly ordered under time pressure
followUps: Where does a connection pool's exhaustion show up in this picture?

questions.prompt: How do you structure tests for a service with ML components - what is worth testing at each level, and what is genuinely different from ordinary software testing?
questions.modelAnswer: The pyramid still applies: many fast unit tests on feature transforms and business logic, integration tests on pipeline and API contracts, and a few end-to-end smoke tests. The ML-specific differences are three. First, model outputs are statistical, so you test properties rather than exact values: output schema and ranges, invariants like monotonicity where the domain demands them, and metric thresholds on a fixed golden set - 'AUC at least X on this fixture' - with float tolerances and pinned seeds instead of assertEqual. Second, data gets first-class tests: schema and distribution validation on inputs, in CI against fixtures and in production against live traffic, because most ML failures arrive through the data path rather than the code path. Third, the model artifact is a versioned dependency: a candidate model bump runs the eval suite in CI exactly as a library bump runs unit tests, with a pinned tiny model keeping the rest of the service's tests fast and deterministic. Add a seeded one-epoch training smoke test so the training loop itself is covered - the classic gap where everything unit-passes while training silently broke.
rubric: Keeps the pyramid but converts model assertions to properties, invariants, and thresholds
Elevates data validation to a first-class test target in CI and production
Treats model updates as dependency bumps gated by evals in CI
Covers the training loop with a seeded smoke test, with determinism handled via pins
followUps: What flakiness sources appear in ML test suites, and how do you quarantine them?

questions.prompt: A feature branch is 30 commits behind main with conflicts. Talk through rebase versus merge for catching it up - and how you recover when a rebase goes wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: Merging main into the branch creates one merge commit, preserves history exactly as it happened, and resolves all conflicts in a single sitting - safe, if noisy. Rebasing replays the branch's commits on top of main for a linear history, but conflicts arrive commit by commit (resolve, git rebase --continue, or --abort to bail out cleanly), and it rewrites commit SHAs - which is why the iron rule is never rebase a branch others are building on, and why pushing afterwards requires force. Use --force-with-lease rather than --force: it refuses to overwrite remote work you have not seen, protecting a teammate who pushed in the meantime. Recovery is where git rewards understanding: the reflog records every previous HEAD position, so git reflog, find the pre-rebase entry, and git reset --hard to it restores the branch exactly - committed work is effectively never lost while the reflog lives. Also worth saying: if the team squash-merges PRs anyway, main's history is linear regardless, and the rebase-versus-merge debate on the feature branch is mostly aesthetics - team convention should win over personal taste.
rubric: Accurate mechanics of both paths, including per-commit conflict resolution and --abort
States the shared-branch rule and prefers --force-with-lease with its rationale
Recovery via reflog and reset is concrete and correct
Frames the choice as team convention, noting squash-merge makes it moot
followUps: When is git rerere worth enabling for repeated conflict resolution?

questions.prompt: Explain image versus container, and why containers displaced VMs for service deployment - including one thing VMs still do better.
questions.modelAnswer: An image is the immutable artifact: a layered filesystem plus metadata - entrypoint, env, exposed ports - built once and shipped everywhere. A container is a running instance of that image: a process (or process tree) on the host, isolated through kernel namespaces (pid, network, mount) and constrained by cgroups, with a thin writable layer on top; one image, many containers. Containers won deployment because they share the host kernel: no guest OS per instance means millisecond starts and dense packing, and the image pins the entire userspace dependency stack, giving dev-prod parity - the durable fix for 'works on my machine' - plus artifact-based rollbacks by redeploying the previous image. What VMs still do better is isolation: a hypervisor boundary with a separate kernel per guest is a far stronger security wall than a shared kernel, where a kernel exploit is a container escape; that is why untrusted multi-tenant code runs in microVMs like Firecracker, and why VMs remain the answer when you need a different OS or kernel than the host. The practical default: containers for your own services, VM-grade isolation where tenants are untrusted.
rubric: Image as immutable layered artifact versus container as namespaced process is precise
Names the shared-kernel mechanism behind speed and density, plus dev-prod parity
Correctly credits VMs with the stronger isolation boundary and the microVM middle ground
Gives the trust-based decision rule at the end
followUps: What actually happens at docker run - which namespaces and cgroups get created?

questions.prompt: A few heavy customers are hammering your inference API. Design rate limiting and caching for it: algorithms, where they live, and the failure modes of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate limiting: token bucket per API key - a capacity for bursts, a refill rate for sustained throughput - which serves real traffic better than fixed windows (burst-at-boundary artifacts) while staying simple to reason about. Enforce at the gateway with counters in a shared store like Redis using atomic operations, and decide the Redis-down behavior deliberately: fail open with conservative local limits for availability, or fail closed where overload is the greater risk. Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers so well-behaved clients back off on their own. Crucially for LLM APIs, requests are long-lived and wildly variable in cost, so per-second request rate is a weak control: cap concurrent in-flight requests per key, and meter token-denominated quotas separately from request rate - the monthly budget and the burst control are different mechanisms. Caching: an exact-match response cache keyed on a canonical hash of model, parameters, and input - but only for deterministic (temperature-zero) requests, because caching sampled outputs silently changes product semantics; below that, engine-level prefix caching accelerates shared system prompts for everyone. Failure modes to design against: unnormalized keys collapsing distinct requests (or missing identical ones), hot-key stampedes on popular prompts - request coalescing so one miss populates for all waiters - and per-tenant fairness inside shared cache capacity so one heavy customer cannot evict everyone else.
rubric: Chooses token bucket with burst/sustain reasoning and distributed atomic enforcement
Makes the fail-open/fail-closed call explicitly and returns actionable 429s
Recognizes long-lived variable-cost requests: concurrency caps and token quotas beside rate
Caches only deterministic outputs with canonical keys, and handles stampedes via coalescing
followUps: How do you communicate limits so heavy customers upgrade instead of churning?

questions.prompt: Ten minutes after your service deploy, the 5xx rate jumps from 0.1 percent to 8 percent and pages fire. What do you do, in order?
questions.modelAnswer: Roll back first, diagnose second: an error spike ten minutes post-deploy is the deploy until proven otherwise, rollback costs minutes while root-causing costs hours, and users are eating errors the entire time you investigate - if the change rode a feature flag, flipping it off is even faster. Verify recovery on the dashboards, post status so nobody duplicates the response, and preserve evidence: keep the bad build and capture logs and traces from the window. Then investigate at leisure: which endpoints and error codes, what the traces say, and the full diff of the deploy - code, config, dependency bumps, and migrations. Migrations are the trapdoor case, because rolling back code does not roll back a schema; that risk is designed away ahead of time with expand-migrate-contract so old and new code both run against the current schema, and it is why 'roll back' must be a rehearsed, known-safe operation rather than a hope. Afterwards, a blameless postmortem with a timeline, and the question that actually improves things: why did no gate catch it - and the fix is usually canary deploys with automatic rollback on error-rate breach, plus the missing test or alert, plus smaller deploys, since rollback-first only works when each deploy is small enough to be safely reversible.
rubric: Rolls back before diagnosing, with the time-asymmetry argument made explicit
Handles the migration trapdoor via expand-migrate-contract compatibility
Preserves evidence and communicates status during mitigation
Postmortem targets the missing gate: canary with auto-rollback, smaller deploys
followUps: What makes a rollback unsafe, and how do you audit for those conditions ahead of time?

questions.prompt: The service passes all tests locally and in CI, but returns 502s through the load balancer in production. How do you debug it?
questions.modelAnswer: A 502 is the load balancer telling you it could not get a valid response from upstream, so first split the problem at the LB: check target health status, and hit the app directly from inside the environment - exec into the pod or port-forward and curl localhost. If direct requests succeed while LB requests fail, it is wiring; if both fail, it is the app in this environment. The classic wiring causes: the app bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 inside the container, so nothing outside the netns can reach it; a port mismatch between containerPort, service, and target group; or a health-check path returning non-200 so every instance gets marked unhealthy and pulled. App-in-this-environment causes: missing env vars or secrets in prod config, OOM crash-looping under a prod-sized memory limit it never sees locally, or an LB idle timeout shorter than a slow endpoint's response time. Read the LB's own logs - they distinguish connection refused from timeout from bad response, which cuts the hypothesis space in half immediately - and walk the request path hop by hop comparing config against what CI exercised, since CI almost never tests the LB-to-container wiring. Fix the class, not the instance: a post-deploy smoke test that hits the service through the load balancer.
rubric: Bisects at the LB with a direct-to-app request before guessing
Names the classic wiring causes: bind address, port mismatch, failing health checks
Uses LB logs' refused/timeout/bad-response distinction as evidence
Prevents recurrence with a through-the-LB smoke test in the pipeline
followUps: Which of these causes would a staging environment have caught, and which slip through to prod anyway?
